headline: Napatree Peanut Bunker Ball Up, Tog Reopens on Crab, Albies Still a Tease
subhead: The breachways are loaded with bait and bluefish are hammering it in daylight — but the stripers and the first albie run are waiting on darkness and the new moon tide.
body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Napatree Point Tuesday evening and watched a peanut bunker school get squeezed against the breachway wall so tight the water looked like it was boiling from underneath — except it wasn't bass doing the boiling, it was blues. That's been the story on this whole stretch of shore the last ten days. The bait is here, it's thick, and it's daytime bluefish cashing in on it while the stripers wait for the sun to go down.

Water along the ocean-facing beaches has been sitting in that low-to-mid-70s range, which is warm enough that the bass have pulled off the immediate structure during daylight and gone nocturnal. I'm not fighting that pattern anymore, I'm fishing it. Best bass action I've had has been after dark off the ledges at Sakonnet Point and the rock piles below the Jamestown bridge — eels on a slow drift, or bunker chunks fished dead-still in the current seams where the rock drops into deeper water. Nothing huge, mostly mid-20s to low-30s inch fish, but they're eating with confidence once the light's gone and the water cools a couple degrees off the surface heat.

Daytime belongs to the blues right now, and they've been aggressive. Second Beach and the beach break off Sakonnet have had bluefish blitzes chasing the same peanut bunker and silversides that are drawing everything else in. Poppers and metal — Kastmasters, half-ounce and up — worked fast across the surface will get bit almost every cast when the birds are diving. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader, because these blues have teeth and they're not shy about using them on 20-pound mono.

Fluke have been the honest bite of the summer and nothing's changed there. Drifting the sandy edges off the Weekapaug reefs and inside the Charlestown breachway on the last of the outgoing tide has been steady — not a blitz, but steady, which is exactly what I expected out of this bite a week ago and exactly what's playing out. Keeper fish mixed with a lot of shorts, four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet. If you're patient and keep moving the drift to find the cleaner sand pockets between the rock piles, you'll put a few in the cooler.

Big one for this time of year — tautog season reopened August 1st, and I've already had two solid outings on green crabs around the humps off Jamestown and the ledge structure outside Newport harbor. Slack tide is when you want to be anchored up tight to the rock, because once the current starts running these fish tuck into the cracks and won't come out for anything. I've been finding fish in 15 to 30 feet, dropping straight down on a jig head tipped with a whole green crab, and letting it sit right on the structure rather than working it. First week back after a closure they're usually a little easier — haven't been pestered in months — so if you've got a tog rod that's been sitting in the garage, now's the window before the crowds figure it out.

Now for the albies — everybody's asking, nobody's seeing them yet. Not at Napatree, not in the Watch Hill breachway, not off Sakonnet. The bait's right, the timing is right, but I haven't had a confirmed sighting of a fin or a tail push through any of the breachways on this stretch. What I will say is the tide is building toward the new moon, and that's exactly the kind of current strength that tends to trigger the first push of albies into structure like Napatree and Watch Hill. I've seen this pattern enough Augusts in a row to trust it — stronger tides mean more bait getting funneled through the breachway mouths, and albies follow bait through a funnel better than almost any other fish we get down here. If I had one morning to burn this week, I'd be standing on the Napatree rocks at first light with an Albie Snax or a small epoxy jig tied on, just in case the first wave shows early.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much change in the next 24 hours — warm surface water, bluefish dominating the daylight hours, bass staying nocturnal along the rocky structure. Where it gets interesting is 48 to 72 hours out, when that new moon tide really starts to load up. That's the window I'd watch closest for the first real albie sign in the breachways, and it's also when I'd expect the striper bite to get a little more aggressive after dark as the stronger current stirs up more bait along the ledges. No reason to change what's working until then — eels and chunks after dark for bass, poppers and metal for blues in the daylight, green crabs on the humps for tog, and Gulp on bucktails for the fluke. Keep an eye on that tide table and don't be surprised if the breachways go from quiet to busy in a hurry once the current really starts to run.
